commitResults.messageTitle: Lower-case the generic user in code comments #641 (#655)
commitResults.messageBody: Address code-quality findings from the pre-release audit (beyond #556)

commitResults.messageTitle: Suggest the long option for a one-dash word
commitResults.messageBody:
Typing `--` autocorrects to an em dash in many editors and on macOS,
and pasting a command out of a document does the same. The tokenizer
folds the dashes it is handed one for one, so a pasted `--phone`
arrives as a single dash before a word, which is no option at all.
The reply says there is no -phone option and stops there, even though
`--Phone` and `-N` are each offered the option they were nearly
spelled as. Anyone whose editor rewrote the dashes is left with
nothing to go on.

Let's count the long option of a word written after one dash among
the spellings that word may stand for, so `--phone` is offered for
`-phone`, and fold case alongside the dashes so it is offered for
`-Phone` too. As before, a spelling is only offered when the command
being parsed supports it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Drop the unreachable leading-dash guard
commitResults.messageBody:
A marker only reaches the near-spelling test from a token the
tokenizer has already read as an option, and a token is an option
only when it opens with a dash. Asking again whether the marker
opens with one is a question with a single possible answer, which
no test can make false and which invites the reader to wonder when
it might be.

Let's ask only whether the marker opens with two dashes, and say in
the comment why one dash is what is left when it does not.

commitResults.messageTitle: Accept adjacent hyphens in email domain labels
commitResults.messageBody:
TAB refuses an email whose domain label holds two hyphens in a row, so
an address such as student@xn--bcher-kva.de cannot be recorded. The
xn-- prefix marks an IDNA A-label (RFC 5890 2.3.2.1), which is a plain
ASCII domain of the kind the User Guide promises to accept, so a
student's real contact address is turned away.

Let's allow a run of hyphens inside a domain label and widen
VALIDATION_REGEX to match, so the hand-written checks and the regex
still agree on the same address. A label still may not be empty, nor
start or end with a hyphen.

commitResults.messageTitle: Read a modifier apostrophe as an apostrophe in names
commitResults.messageBody:
The comparison key behind name search and the possible-duplicate
warning folds the two curly quotation marks onto the straight
apostrophe and nothing else. A roster pasted into TAB carries other
characters where a reader sees an apostrophe: DʼSouza with the
modifier apostrophe, Hawaiʻi with the turned comma, Tatʹyana with the
modifier prime, and the fullwidth apostrophe and the prime that a CJK
keyboard and a spreadsheet leave behind. A TA who types D'Souza on an
ASCII keyboard is told there is no such student, and the User Guide
promises that name searches ignore apostrophe styles.

Let's read every one of them as the straight apostrophe. The grave and
the acute accent stay as they are, because both mark the letter beside
them rather than stand between two letters, which is how this key
already reads the accents it strips.

Two names that differ only in apostrophe style now also warn as
possible duplicates, which is the same promise read from the other
side. The key serves comparison alone, so no stored spelling changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the dot when a domain label is empty
commitResults.messageBody:
An address such as eve@example.com., where a full stop has been pasted
along with the address, is refused with "the last part of the domain
needs at least 2 characters". The last part the reader sees is com,
which has three, so the explanation sends them hunting for a fault
that is not there. A leading dot and a doubled dot are no better off:
they fall through to the general domain message, which never mentions
the dot at all.

Let's answer all three with one reason that names the dot, placed
ahead of the measurement of the last label so an empty tail can no
longer be mistaken for a short one. The addresses stay refused; only
the reason given for refusing them changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fit the startup error dialog on the screen
commitResults.messageBody:
The dialog that reports unreadable saved data grows to whatever height
its wrapped text asks for. A JSON syntax error has it quote the part
of the data file the failure points at, and at 1280x720 with 150%
scaling, a display the course requires us to support, that quotation
makes the dialog taller than the screen. Its heading and its Close TAB
button are then both drawn past the edge of the display, and nothing
scrolls, so neither can be brought back into view.

Let's measure the dialog against the screen it opens on, and give the
message a container that scrolls where the screen has less room than
the message asks for.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the shape the whole data file must have
commitResults.messageBody:
A data file whose outermost value is not an object stops loading with
Jackson's own type error, "Can not deserialize instance of
seedu.tab.storage.JsonSerializableStudentBook out of START_ARRAY
token". Pasting just the list of students into the file is an easy
mistake to make when records are moved between files, and that message
names a storage class and a parser token instead of the one thing the
reader needs to know: the list belongs under a `students` key inside an
object.

Let's read the data file through a JsonUtil entry point that turns down
an outermost value that is not an object, with the caller's own
description of the shape its file should hold. An empty file and a file
holding only null keep the explanations they already have, neither
being a shape the caller can describe usefully.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the shape of the student list and its entries
commitResults.messageBody:
A `students` key holding an object, and an entry in that list holding a
bare name, each stop the data file loading with Jackson's own type
error: "Can not deserialize instance of java.util.ArrayList out of
START_OBJECT token", and "Can not instantiate value of type [simple
type, class seedu.tab.storage.JsonAdaptedStudent] from String value
('Bob')". Neither names the `students` field, and neither tells a
teaching assistant repairing the file that the key takes an array of
records or what a record looks like. A malformed `tags` value already
states both.

Let's read the list through a deserializer that names the field, the
offending entry and the shape each should have, as the tags
deserializer does. An entry written as null, and a field mistake
inside a well-formed record, keep the record number they report.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge upstream/master into 634-explain-a-misshapen-data-file
Keep the student index readable at the minimum width
commitResults.messageBody:
The theme holds the index column on a student card to a fixed 22
pixels, while the card itself asks for whatever width the number needs.
The theme wins. In a window at the smallest size TAB accepts, an index
of three or four digits is drawn as 9... or 1..., and nothing on the
card recovers it, not even a tooltip.

That index is what a reader types into edit, tag and delete, and the
Developer Guide asks the product to hold a thousand records, so the
command target goes missing exactly where the list is long enough to
need it. A different fixed width would only move the problem, since
the room digits take depends on their count, the font and the display
scale.

Let's drop the fixed minimum and leave the index to the preferred-size
minimum the card already sets for it. The name and contacts beside it
give up the few pixels, which is what their layout is there to do.

commitResults.messageTitle: Spell the apostrophe variants as Unicode escapes
commitResults.messageBody:
The seven characters the name comparison key reads as an apostrophe sit
in the source as themselves, and so do the two accents the tests hold
apart from them. Their glyphs are near enough identical that a reviewer
cannot tell which literal is which, nor that a list of them holds no
duplicate and no omission.

Let's write each of them as its Unicode escape, the way this file
already writes the zero-width joiner and the minus sign. The compiler
reads an escape as the character, so nothing about the comparison
changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document how a pasted dash opens an option
commitResults.messageBody:
TAB reads the dashes an editor writes for a typed hyphen as the
option marker, one dash per hyphen, and the User Guide said so
until a merge resolution on the guide rewrite dropped master's
side of the conflict. No commit deletes the bullet, so nothing
points a reader at the rule, and the guide is silent on why a
pasted command behaves differently from a typed one. The
Developer Guide lost its paragraph the same way, and its parser
section still describes the suggestion as a lowercase one.

Let's say in the User Guide that a dash written for a hyphen
opens an option, that each dash stands for one `-` and a single
em dash is therefore refused with the long option suggested, and
that a dash within a value is kept. Let's record the rule for the
tokenizer in the Developer Guide, describe the suggestion as it
now stands, and give the manual testers the em dash to paste.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a manual test for a misshapen data file
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide's hand-edited data tests cover a malformed field
value and a syntax error, but not a file whose structure is the
mistake. A tester following the appendix never checks that TAB explains
a file holding only its list of students, a `students` key holding an
object, or an entry holding a bare value.

Let's add one step covering the three shapes, with the explanation each
should give.

commitResults.messageTitle: Describe the widened apostrophe fold in the DG
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide's Name row says the comparison key ignores curly
apostrophe variants, which is narrower than the key it describes: that
key also reads the fullwidth apostrophe, the prime and three modifier
letters as the straight apostrophe. A developer reading the row is told
less than the code does, and the row disagrees with the User Guide's
own promise that name searches ignore apostrophe styles.

The manual-testing appendix has the matching gap. It walks an en dash
through a search and a possible-duplicate warning, but every name in it
spells an apostrophe the one way an ASCII keyboard does, so nothing
there exercises the fold a pasted roster needs.

Let's say "apostrophe styles" in the row, the wording the User Guide
already uses, and name the accents that stay significant beside the
dash-shaped letter that already does. Let's also walk a modifier letter
apostrophe through the appendix the way the en dash is walked through
it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cap the error dialog as it is laid out
commitResults.messageBody:
The startup error dialog decides how much room its message may have
from a measurement taken before the dialog opens. It is then laid out
with its stylesheet and its fonts applied, so the height it ends up
with can differ from the one that decision was based on, and the cap
it was meant to keep to stops holding. CI reports exactly that on
macOS. A screen shorter than the dialog's own parts need has no answer
at all.

Let's work out the room left for the message each time the dialog is
measured, from the parts drawn around it in that same measurement, and
never leave the message fewer than a few lines to scroll in. Let's
also have the tests report the heights they measured, and stand aside
where the screen is too short for what they check.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge upstream/master into 626-fit-the-startup-error-dialog-on-screen
Keep the error dialog's cap to whole pixels
commitResults.messageBody:
The room the startup error dialog leaves its message is a share of the
screen's height, and on a screen whose share is not a whole number of
pixels the dialog rounds that room up as it draws it. The dialog then
stands a fraction of a pixel above the cap it is held to. CI reports
609.3 asked for and 610 drawn, on a macOS screen 677 pixels tall.

Let's take the room down to a whole pixel before the dialog is given
it, so that rounding cannot carry it past the cap, and let the test
say how far above a cap it will believe a dialog is merely rounded.

commitResults.messageTitle: Warn on a phone written with a country code
commitResults.messageBody:
The possible-duplicate warning compares two phone numbers by their
digits alone, so 8743 8807 and +65 8743 8807 count as different
numbers and adding the second against the first raises nothing. The
User Guide's own add example writes a phone as "+65 9123 4567", which
makes a roster that mixes the local and the international form likely,
and the warning then misses the duplicate it exists to catch.

Let's treat the shorter of two numbers as the same number when it is
the whole tail of the longer one, which covers a country code or a
trunk prefix written in front without naming any one country. The
shorter number needs seven digits of its own, so a short number does
not match every longer one that ends with it, and digits added at the
end stay a different number because they reach a different endpoint.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name a command that flags the student
commitResults.messageBody:
`tag 1 -a "Needs follow-up"` is refused with advice to use
`--follow-up`, and the note on `tag 1 -a "Needs_follow_up"` says the
same. `tag` takes no follow-up option, so following either message
produces a second failure that does not mention `edit` either, leaving
the user to find the right command in the User Guide.

Let's have both messages name the `edit` command that flags the student
the user just addressed, as the hint for taking the label off a flagged
student already does. `add` and `edit` take the option themselves, so
their wording stays as it is.

commitResults.messageTitle: Measure geometry slack in device pixels
commitResults.messageBody:
The window geometry tests allow an edge to stand one logical pixel past
the area it must fit. A window's position and its size each snap to the
device-pixel grid, and an area reduced by desktop panels need not be a
whole number of device pixels, so on a 1920x1200 display at 125% the
window is rounded up twice and two tests fail on a developer's own
desktop while passing on CI and under a plain Xvfb.

Let's count the slack in device pixels instead, report the scale beside
the measurements when an assertion fails, and pin the geometry such a
display produces so the rule holds where no window manager runs to
reproduce it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Attach the slack Javadoc to the method it describes
commitResults.messageBody:
The Javadoc for the device-pixel slack helper sits above the arithmetic
regression test instead of above the helper, because the test was added
between the two. It describes a return value and a scale argument, so on
a void test method it describes nothing.

Let's put it back on snapAllowance, where the return value and the
argument it names both exist.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say which phones match, and show it in a test
commitResults.messageBody:
The guide says two phones match when one is the other behind a country
code. The rule is wider: the whole of the shorter number has to be the
end of the longer one, so a number from another country ending in the
same digits is matched too, and a reader told only about country codes
would not expect that warning.

The manual-testing appendix cannot show the rule either. Its one phone
example writes the same digits on both records, so it raised a warning
before this change as well.

Let's describe the rule the code applies and name the case it catches by
accident, and add a step whose records differ until the new rule is
applied, beside one whose trailing digits keep it silent.

commitResults.messageTitle: Leave the manual-testing appendix as it stands
commitResults.messageBody:
The step added alongside the guide wording walks a local number and its
country-code form through the duplicate warning. The appendix already
runs long, and every step a tester has to read costs attention that the
cases carrying more risk need.

Let's drop that step and keep the appendix the size it was. The rule it
would have shown is stated in the User Guide and pinned by unit tests.

commitResults.messageTitle: Describe how phones are compared
commitResults.messageBody:
The guide's phone bullet runs to three sentences where its neighbours
run to one, and tells the reader to weigh a warning, which the bullet
below it already does. The Developer Guide still says duplicate
warnings compare the digits of a phone, which stopped holding when the
tail rule arrived.

Let's split that bullet in two and drop what the next one covers, and
record in the Developer Guide which comparison the warnings use and why
an unrelated number ending in the same digits reaches it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Measure the compact window's scene, not its frame
commitResults.messageBody:
MainWindowTest.resize_shortWindow_keepsStudentAndHelpFootersReachable
asks the window to shrink to 400 pixels and then reads the stage
height to confirm that it did. The stage height counts the title bar
the window manager draws, so on a desktop running one the assertion
sees 429.6 against a limit of 400 and fails, while a plain Xvfb draws
no frame and CI passes. The gap is a decoration tens of device pixels
tall, well beyond the three the geometry slack allows on purpose, so
widening the slack would stop a window that truly overflows failing.

The footers the test goes on to check are laid out in the scene, as is
every other node it measures.

Let's compare the scene height against the minimum instead, and name
both heights in the message so a later failure says which box grew.

Document equivalence partitions in test case comments

which makes partition and boundary coverage harder to review.

Let's clarify those groups beside existing test cases while preserving

commitResults.messageTitle: Point the DG's file-editing link at the UG section
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide's data contract section links to
UserGuide.md#editing-the-data-file. No element carries that ID, because
the User Guide rewrite renamed the section to "Saving and editing
data". A reader following the link for the JSON fields and the recovery
instructions lands at the top of the guide instead, with no sign of
where the promised section went.

Let's point the link at #saving-and-editing-data, the only dead anchor
among the 11 documents under docs/.

commitResults.messageTitle: Point the DG's file-editing link at the UG section #629 (#677)
commitResults.messageBody: DG file-editing cross-reference points to a missing UG section

commitResults.messageTitle: Close three wording gaps in the User Guide
commitResults.messageBody:
Three things a reader meets in the guide give less than they could.

The name TAB is expanded only in the Developer Guide, so a reader of
the User Guide or the product website is never told what it stands
for. The FAQ's save-lock answer opens on a test of the error text,
which the reader must hold in mind before reaching the instruction.
The `find` note states that names treat dashes as spaces while other
fields do not, without saying why, so the asymmetry reads as an
oversight rather than a decision.

Let's expand the name on first use, as "Teaching Assistant's Book" to
match the Developer Guide, lead the lock answer with the situation
instead of the test, and give the dash rule its reason.

commitResults.messageTitle: Point edit's missing-target reply at --target-id
commitResults.messageBody:
In edit, --id sets the NUS Student ID field and --target-id selects the
student by ID, while delete and tag select with --id. A user who carries
that habit over and runs edit --id A01234567X -p 91234567 reads "Missing
required field(s): INDEX or NUS_STUDENT_ID", which contradicts the ID
they just typed and never names the option that would have worked. The
User Guide selects with --id in its delete and tag examples, so the
mistake is an easy one to make, and a digit-leading edit --id 1234 gets
the same bare reply.

Let's explain the asymmetry when edit is given the ID field but no
target: say that --id sets a new ID and that --target-id selects the
student holding one. A command that names no target and no ID field
keeps its existing reply, so only the confusing case gains the pointer.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cover OPTION=VALUE and quote escaping in help
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide's command format section says the built-in help
reference covers additional syntax, including OPTION=VALUE and
escaping quotation marks. The reference's input rules mention
neither, so a reader who follows that pointer finds nothing, even
though TAB accepts both forms.

Let's add an attached-value rule and a backslash escaping rule to
the input rules, each with an example, so the reference delivers
what the guide promises.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep Hangul syllables whole in the name key
commitResults.messageBody:
The comparison key that name search and the possible-duplicate warning
share decomposes a name to NFD and then drops only the Latin marks it
finds. A Hangul syllable decomposes into letters rather than marks, so
nothing puts one back together: 이 is left as the two letters 임 opens
with, which makes find -n 이 answer with 임지수 as well as 이서연, and
find -n 기 answer with 김민준, a name that holds no such syllable. 이 is
one of the most common Korean surnames, so a roster of Korean students
cannot be searched by it.

Let's compose the key back to NFC once the marks are gone. A mark that
is already dropped cannot return, so Latin accents, strokes and the
apostrophe styles fold as they did.

commitResults.messageTitle: Read a blank-looking edit value as a clear
commitResults.messageBody:
Edit reads a quoted value as a request to clear a detail when
String.trim leaves nothing of it, and that test strips nothing above
U+0020. The full-width space a CJK input method types and the
non-breaking space a paste carries both sit above it, so a value the
user sees as blank clears every tag but is refused for the phone, the
email and the ID. The email and ID refusals quote "", the very
spelling the User Guide gives for clearing a detail, so the reply
contradicts the guide it sends the reader back to.

Let's ask StringUtil.normalizeFieldValue whether the value is blank,
the question the tag path already asks, so all four options read a
blank-looking value the same way.

commitResults.messageTitle: Simplify the lock and dash wording from review
commitResults.messageBody:
The lock answer opens by naming what TAB does before naming the file it
does it with, which asks the reader to hold a clause before the thing
it describes. The dash rule spells out what the example below it
already shows, and states the reason as something rosters do rather
than as something that happens to a name.

Let's lead the lock sentence with the file, and let the dash rule state
its reason from the name's side and stop at the negation.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'master' into 680-clarify-ui-names-comments
Stop documenting symbolic links to the data file
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide says Storage follows symbolic links before choosing
the lock path, and its manual tests ask testers to link data/tab.json
to a file elsewhere. A link is the user's own file-system setup rather
than a path TAB chooses, so pointing it outside the home folder is out
of scope. Describing and testing links invites readers to treat them as
a supported feature, and the target the test uses sits outside the
data folder.

Let's drop the symbolic-link sentence from "Saving changes safely" and
the symbolic-link manual test.

commitResults.messageTitle: Hold one index column width across the list
commitResults.messageBody:
The index on a student card is sized to its own text, so the text
beside it starts wherever that card's number ends. A list of ten or
more students therefore reads with a ragged left edge: the names on
cards 1 to 9 start a digit's width further left than the name on card
10. The fixed column this replaced was removed because it cut off
three- and four-digit indices, so putting it back is no answer.

Let's reserve the column with an invisible copy of the widest index
the list can show, which JavaFX lays out in the card's real font at
any display scale. The real index keeps its own minimum, so a long one
still widens the column rather than being cut off, and the list
rebuilds its cards when that width changes, since a cell holding an
unchanged student is not rebuilt on its own.

commitResults.messageTitle: Clarify UI names and source comments #680 (#693)
commitResults.messageBody: Clarify UI variable names and source comments from the code audit

commitResults.messageTitle: Hold the reserved index width under pressure
commitResults.messageBody:
The invisible index reserves the column with a preferred width, which a
card short of room is free to take back. Where it does, each card falls
back to the width of its own index and the ragged column returns: on a
320 pixel list, nine single-digit cards start their names four pixels
left of the tenth. That is the width the list has when the window sits
at its own minimum, so the alignment went missing exactly where the
window is narrowest.

Let's hold the reserved width as the invisible index's minimum as well,
and measure the narrow widths with a name long enough to want more room
than the card has.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cover an ID the field cannot hold
commitResults.messageBody:
A comment in the missing-target test calls 1A2B3C a value that is no
valid ID. The field takes 1 to 32 ASCII letters or digits in any order,
so that is a valid ID and the case it claims to cover is untested: both
inputs beside it are ordinary IDs.

Let's say what those inputs are, and add a value no ID could hold, so
the reply is pinned where the pointer and the field's own reason are
given together.

commitResults.messageTitle: Build the alignment IDs free of the machine locale
commitResults.messageBody:
The narrow-layout regression formats its NUS Student IDs with the
default locale, which writes its own digits where it has them. Under
ar-EG the fixture asks for the ID A٠٠٠٠٠٠١X, which the field refuses,
so the builder throws before a single name is measured and the test
reports a locale fault rather than the alignment it guards.

Let's format those IDs with Locale.ROOT, as the rest of the project
formats the numbers it shows.

commitResults.messageTitle: Settle on one notion of a blank value in edit
commitResults.messageBody:
EditCommandParser asks three times whether a value holds anything, and
answers differently each time. The clearable fields ask field
normalization, which reads every Unicode space as blank. The ID field
test and the two selector sites ask String.isBlank and String.trim,
which count only the spaces Java calls whitespace, so a no-break space
reads as a value the user meant. A selector holding one is answered
"Index must be a positive integer", about a kind of value the command
does not contain; one beside --target-id is refused as a second target;
and an ID field holding one is told how to select a student, although
the same command clears that field.

No user meets any of this, because the command box turns every Unicode
space into an ordinary one before the parser reads it. It is a defect
waiting for a second way in.

Let's ask the one question everywhere, through a named helper, so the
three sites cannot drift apart again.

commitResults.messageTitle: Suggest an option behind any number of dashes
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide says TAB suggests a correction for an option given with
the wrong number of dashes. One direction does: a word behind a single
dash, which is what a word processor leaves when it autocorrects --.
A letter behind two dashes gets nothing, so --p, --e and --t are
refused by name with no way back to -p, -e and -t, and neither do the
extra dashes a held key leaves, as in ---phone.

Let's read the name rather than the dashes it arrives behind, and
offer that name behind the dashes an option of its length carries. A
lone letter after one dash is a whole short option already, so it
keeps its own spelling and is never offered a long one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Offer a short alias longer than one letter
commitResults.messageBody:
The correction reads a name's length to decide the dashes it belongs
behind, one letter taking one dash and anything longer taking two. A
short option is as long as its command spells it, and --no-follow-up
answers to -nf, so --nf and ---nf are refused by name with no way back
to the alias that works.

Let's offer the name behind both runs and let the command say which it
spells, keeping one letter away from a long spelling because no long
option is a single letter.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cover the guard against dashes carrying no name
commitResults.messageBody:
The correction reads the name a marker carries and offers it behind
each dash run, so it checks first that there is a name at all. Nothing
exercises that check, and a bare -- is an option a user can type, so
the branch that keeps dashes alone from being offered every spelling
goes untested.

Let's drive -- and --- through the tokenizer.

commitResults.messageTitle: Reveal the whole of a newly added card
commitResults.messageBody:
The reveal that follows an add scrolls once per layout pass and stops
after two of them, on the count rather than on the card. A card whose
contact row wraps grows once it has a width to wrap against, which
happens after the scroll that revealed it, so the bottom of the card
is left below the edge of the list with nothing to scroll to it again.
On a 740 by 600 window such a card reaches 19 pixels past the list it
sits in, and it is the card the user just asked to see.

Let's scroll until the whole card is in view, keeping the count as the
stop for a card taller than the list, which no scrolling can show
whole.

commitResults.messageTitle: Count one more pass rather than ask about the card
commitResults.messageBody:
Scrolling until the whole card is in view needs a helper that asks
whether it is, and three of the branches that helper takes cannot be
reached: every node under .list-cell is a cell, and a card the list
has just scrolled to is never above its top. The patch coverage gate
refuses them, and tests written only to reach branches that cannot
fail would buy the gate off rather than say anything.

Measuring says the heights settle by the third pass, and the fourth
already in place is margin.

Let's keep the count, and record in the comment what was measured and
what the count still assumes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Check that a revealed card stays in view
commitResults.messageBody:
The regression for #707 waits for the whole of a new card to be inside
the list, and finishes at the first pass where it is. A card in a window
of the minimum height is wholly in view for one pass before its contact
row wraps and pushes its bottom back under the edge, so a reveal that
settles on a clipped card still satisfies the test.

Let's count the passes the card spends in view, require sixteen in a
row, and add the short window that the arrival-only check misses.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say a digit-leading target is read as an index
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide's "Choosing a student" gives the explicit ID option for
an ID beginning with a digit, but says nothing about what a bare target
beginning with one does. It is read as a displayed index, so a user who
records such an ID and targets it bare acts on whoever holds that
index, and the guide leaves them no way to learn why.

Let's say so beside the rule it qualifies, with both outcomes: a target
that is a plausible index, and one that is not.

commitResults.messageTitle: Show the refused target as a value, not a command
commitResults.messageBody:
UserGuideExamplesTest parses every backticked command the guide shows
and fails on one the app refuses, which is the rule to keep: a guide
handing out a command that does not work is a bug. The new bullet
quotes the error a digit-leading target draws and writes the target as
a whole delete command, so the guide and the test contradict.

Let's name the refused value on its own, which is what the bullet is
about, and leave the test as strict as it is.

commitResults.messageTitle: Trim the digit-leading target bullet
commitResults.messageBody:
The bullet on digit-leading targets runs to two long sentences and
quotes a whole error message, where the bullets around it state one
rule and give one short example. TAB prints that message at the moment
it matters, so the guide carries it for nothing.

Let's state the rule once and keep the example for the silent case,
which is the one a reader cannot discover by trying.

commitResults.messageTitle: Split the target rule from what to do about it
commitResults.messageBody:
The bullet on digit-leading targets states the rule and the remedy in
one sentence joined by "so", which buries the part a reader acts on.

Let's take the remedy out as its own sentence, addressed to the reader,
as @CJBuzz suggests in review.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document planned whole-tag matching
commitResults.messageBody:
Tag searches match partial values, so a search for T1 also finds
students tagged T10, T11, or T12. The Developer Guide does not
record a planned solution for selecting one complete tag name.

Let's add a Planned Enhancements appendix describing the limitation
and future case-insensitive whole-tag matching with an equals prefix.

commitResults.messageTitle: Clarify partial tag matching in the UG
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide describes partial matching without explaining how
similarly named tutorial tags affect search results. A TA searching
for T1 can therefore also see students from T10, T11, or T12.

Let's add an explicit example of this limitation to the find section.

commitResults.messageTitle: Explain model and utility test partitions
commitResults.messageBody:
Validation and collection tests use representative inputs without
always explaining the behavior groups or their boundaries. This makes
it harder to distinguish new partition coverage from repeated examples.

Let's document the accepted and rejected value groups, identity states,
and boundary representatives while preserving the existing assertions.

commitResults.messageTitle: Explain command parser test partitions
commitResults.messageBody:
Parser tests combine missing values, malformed values, and ambiguous
target forms without always identifying the distinction at each group.
Reviewers have to reconstruct why each representative is present.

Let's describe the syntax and value partitions beside their cases and
identify accepted and rejected index and identifier boundaries.

commitResults.messageTitle: Explain storage and interaction test partitions
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage and interaction tests exercise several data shapes and object
states within shared assertion groups. Their representative values do
not always reveal which behavior distinction each group exercises.

Let's document persisted value shapes, confirmation states, and display
boundaries without changing the inputs, assertions, or application.

commitResults.messageTitle: Match collection test comment style
commitResults.messageBody:
The partition comments in CollectionUtilTest use full sentences beside
retained lowercase fragments, which makes the file read inconsistently.

Let's match the existing lowercase fragment style while preserving the
partition distinctions, test inputs, and assertions.

commitResults.messageTitle: Clarify blank contact clearing comments
commitResults.messageBody:
The email and phone clearing comments describe only quoted empty
strings, but the adjacent success tests also accept quoted whitespace.
This understates the accepted partition.

Let's describe both empty and whitespace-only quoted values while
preserving the test inputs and assertions.

commitResults.messageTitle: Reject options glued to quoted values
commitResults.messageBody:
An option followed immediately by a quoted value is treated as
positional name text by add, silently saving an incorrect name and
omitting the intended field.

Let's recognize a leading unquoted option marker even when a later
part of its token is quoted, so the typo is rejected consistently.
Keep quoted literal values and space- or equals-separated fields,
and cover record and file preservation with regression tests.

commitResults.messageTitle: Clarify UI names and source comments
commitResults.messageBody:
The name-update guard describes truncation even when it restores the
full name, and the width variables obscure their allocation roles.
Repeated overlay explanations and an overly broad logging claim also
make the code harder to read.

Let's name the guard and widths for their purpose, name the clamp's
lower bound, and shorten comments to the guarantees and JavaFX details
that matter, preserving application behavior.

commitResults.messageTitle: Align glued-option coloring with parsing
commitResults.messageBody:
A glued quoted value is colored as a quoted value even though the
parser rejects its unquoted leading option marker. This makes the
command box disagree with submission behavior.

Let's give a leading option marker precedence over later quotes,
preserving quoted literals and equals-attached values, and cover the
coloring distinction with regression tests and manual testing steps.

commitResults.messageTitle: Clarify user guide targets and input rules
commitResults.messageBody:
The guide leaves tag and delete ID options ambiguous and omits field
constraints and input rules documented by earlier fixes. Readers cannot
predict which values TAB accepts or safely edit every supported field.

Let's distinguish command-specific targets, state email and tag rules,
and restore concise guidance for quoting, saved files and launch limits.

commitResults.messageTitle: Simplify user guide rules after review
commitResults.messageBody:
The guide repeats target syntax and includes technical details that
make routine command and field rules harder for users to find.

Let's group field guidance by field, use consistent target wording,
and trim repeated explanations and uncommon implementation details.

commitResults.messageTitle: Explain email syntax and place launch guidance
commitResults.messageBody:
The email warning lacks its standards-based rationale, and launch
advice is separated from the steps users follow to open TAB.

Let's explain why dotless domains are saved, make escape sequences
explicit, and place double-click guidance beside the launch command.

commitResults.messageTitle: Remove the known issues section from the guide
commitResults.messageBody:
The known issues section only links to the issue tracker and adds no
usage guidance beyond the rest of the guide.

Let's remove the section as requested during review.
